Work-energy theorem; kinetic and potential energy

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Conservative forces (gravity, spring, electrostatic) do path-independent work and allow potential energy definition. Non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance) dissipate energy as heat. The general energy equation W_nc = ΔE_mech handles both types — if W_nc = 0, mechanical energy is conserved.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Conservative force: work depends only on endpoints; ∮F·dr = 0 (closed loop)
Non-conservative force: work depends on path; ∮F·dr ≠ 0
Work-energy relation: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Friction does NOT have a potential energy. Many students try to write U_friction = μmgx or something similar. This is WRONG — friction is non-conservative, and the energy it 'removes' from the mechanical system becomes heat, not stored potential energy.  ·  A force being 'conservative' does NOT mean the total energy of the system is conserved. It means mechanical energy can be conserved IF that force is the ONLY force doing work. If you have conservative forces PLUS non-conservative forces, mechanical energy is not conserved even though some forces are conservative.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Friction does NOT have a potential energy — the energy becomes heat, not stored PE.  ·  A conservative force does NOT guarantee energy conservation if non-conservative forces are also present.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Gravity is conservative: Lift a 5 kg mass 3 m up and lower it down. Net work = 0 (closed loop).  ·  Friction is non-conservative: Slide a 2 kg block 5 m on a surface (μ_k = 0.3). Work = −0.3 × 2 × 9.8 × 5 = −29.4 J (depends on path length).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Normal force and tension are NOT conservative forces — they are constraint forces that do zero work (they are perpendicular to displacement). They don't appear in the energy equation because W = 0, not because they have potential energy.  ·  The term 'non-conservative' does NOT mean 'energy is destroyed.' It means mechanical energy is converted to other forms (heat, sound) that are NOT tracked by potential energy. Total energy is ALWAYS conserved (first law).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 problems classifying forces as conservative or non-conservative using the closed-loop test.  ·  Solve 5 mixed-system problems using W_nc = ΔE_mech.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Closed-loop test: if net work around a closed path is zero, the force is conservative.  ·  Path-independence shortcut: gravity, spring, and electrostatic forces are always conservative.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 2 kg block slides 5 m on a rough surface (μ_k = 0.3). Find the work done by friction and the thermal energy generated.  ·  A 1 kg ball is dropped from 20 m. Air resistance does −15 J of work. Find the speed at the ground.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The closed-loop test is the standard way to justify whether a force is conservative.  ·  Gravity, spring, and electrostatic forces are always conservative — memorize these.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: A force is conservative if the work done depends only on initial and final positions, not the path.  ·  The work done by a conservative force around any closed loop is zero: ∮F·dr = 0.  ·  Non-conservative forces dissipate mechanical energy as heat, sound, or deformation.  ·  The general energy equation: W_nc = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Conservative forces (gravity, spring, electrostatic) allow potential energy definition.  ·  Non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance) dissipate energy as heat.  ·  The closed-loop test: if net work around a closed path is zero, the force is conservative.  ·  When both types act, use W_nc = ΔE_mech (general energy equation).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The fundamental forces of nature (gravity, electromagnetism, strong, weak) are all conservative at the fundamental level. Non-conservative forces like friction are emergent — they arise from many conservative interactions at the microscopic level, with energy going into microscopic degrees of freedom (heat).  ·  Noether's theorem: Conservation of energy is linked to time translation symmetry. Conservative forces are those derived from a potential that is time-independent. Time-dependent forces (like a time-varying field) can be non-conservative even if they are fundamental.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Explain why gravity is conservative but friction is not, using the closed-loop test.  ·  A spring (k = 400 N/m) is compressed 0.15 m and released. Find the maximum speed of a 0.5 kg mass.  ·  A 3 kg block slides down a rough 30° slope (μ_k = 0.2) of length 6 m. Find the speed at the bottom.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Friction and air resistance are always non-conservative — they dissipate energy.  ·  Mixed systems (conservative + non-conservative) use W_nc = ΔE_mech.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Mixed system: A 1 kg ball falls 10 m through air. Gravity does +98 J, air resistance does −20 J. Net work = 78 J = ΔK.  ·  Spring is conservative: Compress a spring (k = 500 N/m) by 0.2 m. Work done = ½kx² = 10 J stored as elastic PE.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Which of the following is a conservative force? → C  ·  A block slides 5 m on a rough surface (μ_k = 0.3) and returns to its starting point. The net work done by friction is: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Conservative force definition:** A force is conservative if the work done by it depends ONLY on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. Equivalently, the work done around any closed loop is zero: ∮F·dr = 0.  ·  **Path independence:** For a conservative force, W = U_i - U_f = -(U_f - U_i) = -ΔU. The work is the negative of the change in potential energy. This means we can define a potential energy function U(r) such that F = -∇U (force is the negative gradient of potential).  ·  **Examples of conservative forces:** Gravity (near Earth: F = -mg, U = mgh), spring force (F = -kx, U = ½kx²), electrostatic force (F = kQq/r², U = kQq/r), uniform electric field (F = qE, U = qEy).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Conservative forces allow potential energy definition: F = −∇U.  ·  Conservative force and PE: W = −ΔU (work = negative change in potential energy)  ·  Friction work: W_f = −μNd (always negative; energy dissipated as heat)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Friction always does negative work — it removes mechanical energy from the system.  ·  Air resistance (drag) is non-conservative. The work done by drag depends on the path (speed profile). You CANNOT define a 'drag potential energy.' The energy lost to drag becomes heat in the air.  ·  Closed loop test: A 3 kg block slides around a 2 m × 2 m square (μ_k = 0.2). Net work = −0.2 × 3 × 9.8 × 8 = −47 J ≠ 0 (non-conservative).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The closed-loop test is the definitive way to classify a force as conservative or not.  ·  Normal force is conservative (work = 0 when displacement is perpendicular).  ·  NEB frequently asks: 'Is this force conservative? Justify using the closed-loop test.'

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Friction shortcut: always non-conservative — work = −μNd (depends on path length).  ·  Mixed systems: use W_nc = ΔE_mech — identify non-conservative forces first.  ·  PE definition: only conservative forces allow U to be defined (F = −∇U).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB asks both numerical problems and conceptual questions about force classification.  ·  A 10 kg block slides on a rough horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3) from x=0 to x=5 m, then returns to x=0. Find total work done by friction. Solution: W_going = -μmgd = -0.3×10×9.8×5 = -147 J. W_returning = -147 J. Total W = -294 J ≠ 0. Friction is non-conservative. The energy is dissipated as heat.  ·  A 2 kg mass falls 10 m in air with air resistance. Its speed at the bottom is 12 m/s (instead of 14 m/s without air resistance). Find the work done by air resistance. Solution: Without drag: v = √(2gh) = √(196) = 14 m/s, KE = 196 J. With drag: KE = ½×2×144 = 144 J. Work by drag = ΔKE - W_gravity = 144 - 196 = -52 J.…
